scenes.heading: Metals and alloys
scenes.sub: What makes metals strong, shiny and great conductors?
scenes.say: Bridges, cars, wires, coins and cooking pots are all made of metal. So what makes metals strong, shiny and such good conductors?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.science: Positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
scenes.breaks: Islands stay put, but metal ions vibrate, and their layers really can slide when the metal bends.
scenes.say: Picture islands in a sea. The islands are positive metal ions in a lattice, and the sea is delocalised electrons flowing all around them. The attraction between the ions and the electrons is metallic bonding.

scenes.heading: Why metals behave like metals
points: Conduct: electrons are free to move
scenes.say: This model explains the properties. Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons are free to move. They're malleable and ductile because layers of ions can slide while the electron sea holds them together. And they have high melting points because the attraction is strong.

scenes.heading: The reactivity series
steps: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al
scenes.say: The reactivity series ranks metals from most to least reactive: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium, then carbon, then zinc, iron, tin and lead, then hydrogen, and finally copper, silver and gold. More reactive metals lose their outer electrons more easily.
scenes.caption: The reactivity series ranks metals from most to least reactive: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg and Al, then carbon, then Zn, Fe, Sn and Pb, then hydrogen, and finally Cu, Ag and Au. More reactive metals lose their outer electrons more easily.

scenes.heading: Displacement
scenes.question: Will a reaction occur when iron is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution?
lines: Iron is above copper in the series
Yes: brown copper forms, blue fades
scenes.say: Displacement is a takeover: a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound. Iron is above copper, so iron in copper sulfate makes iron sulfate and copper. Brown copper coats the iron, and the blue solution fades. Copper could never push out iron.

scenes.heading: Getting metals from ores
scenes.say: Most metals are found in ores as compounds. Removing the oxygen is called reduction. Metals above carbon, like aluminium, need electrolysis. Metals below carbon, like iron, are heated with carbon, which takes the oxygen away, in a blast furnace.

scenes.heading: Alloys and rust
points: Alloy: different-sized atoms jam the layers
So alloys are harder than pure metals
Rust needs BOTH oxygen AND water
scenes.say: In an alloy, atoms of a different size jam the layers so they can't slide, so the alloy is harder. Steel is iron with a little carbon. Iron rusts only with both oxygen and water. In galvanising, a zinc coating takes the hit, because zinc is more reactive than iron.

points: Metal ions in a sea of electrons
More reactive metals displace less reactive
Alloys are harder than pure metals
scenes.say: Quick recap. Metals are positive ions in a sea of electrons. More reactive metals displace less reactive ones. Above carbon means electrolysis. Alloys are harder, and rust needs oxygen and water. Now try the practice questions!
